faq.a: A 12‑lead ECG, as it is cheap, rapid and can detect STEMI.
faq.q: What is the first test you should do for chest pain in a low‑resource setting?

faq.a: It confirms myocardial injury quickly, guiding urgent therapy.
faq.q: Why is a point‑of‑care troponin useful?

faq.a: If the patient is haemodynamically stable, has no dyspnoea and the ECG is normal.
faq.q: When can you safely defer a chest X‑ray?

exam: A 28‑year‑old man presents with crushing chest pain radiating to the left arm. What is the next step? — Obtain a 12‑lead ECG immediately; if ST‑segment elevation >1mm in two contiguous leads, give thrombolysis if PCI unavailable.
A patient with hypertension and dyspnoea has a new holosystolic murmur. What is the most likely diagnosis? — Rheumatic mitral regurgitation; confirm with echocardiography if available.
A 45‑year‑old HIV‑positive patient has fatigue and pitting oedema. What is the first investigation? — Baseline ECG and echocardiography to assess for cardiomyopathy.
A 60‑year‑old woman with chest pain and a normal ECG but elevated troponin. What is the diagnosis? — Non‑ST‑segment elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI).
A patient with sudden syncope and a new harsh systolic murmur. What is the red flag? — Possible aortic dissection; call emergency services immediately.
A 35‑year‑old man with palpitations has a regular tachycardia at 140 bpm. What is the first drug to give? — A beta‑blocker to control rate and reduce myocardial oxygen demand.
A patient with heart failure has worsening oedema despite diuretics. What is the next step? — Add a loop diuretic or increase dose; consider ACE inhibitor if not contraindicated.
A 50‑year‑old man with chest pain has a normal troponin but a new ST‑segment depression. What does this suggest? — Ischemia; consider urgent coronary angiography if resources allow.
ai.title: Approach to Cardiovascular Symptoms
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: A structured bedside method to evaluate chest pain, dyspnoea, palpitations and swelling in low‑resource settings. It prioritises common tropical causes, simple bedside tests and rapid red‑flag recognition.

b: History of pain character, timing, radiation, precipitating factors
Physical signs: pulse, BP, jugular venous pressure, peripheral oedema, murmurs
sections.p: Cardiovascular symptoms encompass any complaint suggesting heart or vascular disease: chest pain, breathlessness, palpitations, oedema, syncope. Diagnosis starts with a focused history and physical exam, then simple investigations.

b: ST‑segment elevation, troponin, ECG changes, risk factors, age
sections.p: Use clinical staging to guide urgency. For heart failure, use NYHA class; for chest pain, use the 5‑point risk stratification (ST‑segment change, troponin, ECG, risk factors, age).

In East Africa, the top causes of cardiovascular symptoms are infections and rheumatic disease, followed by hypertension, HIV‑related cardiomyopathy, malaria‑induced myocarditis and herbal cardiotoxins.

b: Chest pain: pressure, crushing, radiates to arm
sections.p: Symptoms vary with pathology: angina is pressure‑like, dyspnoea is exertional, palpitations are irregular, oedema is pitting and often bilateral.
Prioritise tests that are affordable and available. Use bedside tools first, then send samples if possible.

t.b: ST‑segment elevation >1mm in two contiguous leads = STEMI
EF <40% = systolic dysfunction; valve regurgitation/stenosis visible

sections.p: Certain features mandate immediate action: haemodynamic instability, ongoing chest pain, new murmurs, sudden syncope, severe dyspnoea.

b: Revascularise STEMI with thrombolysis if PCI unavailable
ACE inhibitor or ARB for heart failure
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then provide supportive care. Drug choices consider availability, cost and safety.
Regular monitoring of BP, weight, symptoms and adherence to therapy. Counsel on diet, salt restriction, smoking cessation and malaria prevention.

b: Pneumonia – cough, fever, unilateral chest pain
Pulmonary embolism – sudden dyspnoea, pleuritic pain
sections.p: Many non‑cardiac conditions mimic cardiac symptoms: pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, pericarditis, anxiety, thyrotoxicosis.

b: AF may have normal ECG baseline
Orthostatic hypotension missed if supine BP only
Early HF may have normal CXR
sections.p: Low troponin in early ACS, normal ECG in atrial fibrillation, normal BP in orthostatic hypotension, normal chest X‑ray in early heart failure.
